passages.title: Moving to the city
passages.text: Next month my family is moving from a small town to the capital. My father got a new job downtown, and he starts on the first of June. We're going to rent an apartment in a quiet neighborhood near a subway station, so my parents won't need the car every day. I'm excited, but I'm also a little nervous. In my town, everything is close and people know each other. In the city, the streets are crowded and noisy, and the traffic jams can be terrible. My cousin, who lives there, says her commute to school takes almost an hour. However, she loves the parks, the museums and the free concerts on Sundays. She has promised that she will show me around during our first weekend. I think I'm going to miss my old friends, but we'll have a video call every week. Maybe city life won't be so bad after all.

exercises.prompt: What does 'neighborhood' mean in 'I live in a quiet neighborhood'?

points: «be going to» + verbo habla de planes ya decididos y de lo que ves venir: «They're going to build a new line».
«commute» es el trayecto diario al trabajo o a la escuela; también es verbo: «I commute by bus».
Mudarse a otra ciudad es «move to»: «We moved to Chicago».

mistake.wrong: I go to my work in bus.
mistake.right: I go to work by bus.
mistake.note: El medio de transporte va con «by»: «by bus», «by subway». Y se dice «go to work», sin «my».

points: «will» + verbo para decisiones del momento y promesas: «I'll help you».
«be going to» + verbo para planes que ya decidiste: «We're going to move».
Presente continuo para citas y planes acordados: «I'm meeting my friends tonight».
«rent» es el alquiler y también el verbo alquilar: «The rent is too high».

mistake.note: En español el presente sirve para el futuro; en inglés, un plan acordado va en presente continuo.
